title: Intersecting a Borel with a torus centralizer gives a Borel of the centralizer
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $F$, and all subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness mean [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. A group is solvable if its successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups eventually become trivial; a Borel subgroup is a maximal smooth connected solvable subgroup. A torus is a group isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for some integer $r\geq0$, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ for a commutative $F$-algebra $A$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $G$ be smooth and connected, let $B\subseteq G$ be a Borel subgroup, and let $S\subseteq B$ be a torus, not necessarily maximal. Define the centralizer functor by
$$C_G(S)(A)=\{g\in G(A):g_{A'}s=sg_{A'}\text{ for every commutative }A\text{-algebra }A'\text{ and }s\in S(A')\}.$$
This functor is represented by a smooth connected closed subgroup scheme $C\subseteq G$. The scheme-theoretic intersection $B\cap C=B\times_G C$, viewed as a closed subgroup scheme of $C$, is a Borel subgroup of $C$.

source.place: Theorem 17.46 and its proof, printed pp.365--366; restatement 17.72, printed p.376. Smoothness and connectedness are Corollary 13.10 and Theorem 17.38, as explicitly invoked in that proof.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-torus-centralizer-smooth-connected] to $G$ and also to the smooth connected group $B$. Over the algebraically closed field $F$, connectedness is the algebraic-closure test for geometric connectedness [lem-weil-geometrically-connected-algebraic-closure]. Thus $C=C_G(S)$ and $H=C_B(S)$ are represented by smooth connected closed subgroups. On every algebra $A$, both $H(A)$ and $(B\times_G C)(A)$ consist of the elements of $B(A)$ commuting with $S$ after every further algebra extension; the fibre-product universal property identifies $H=B\cap C$ as subgroup schemes [def-pc-fibre-product]. The derived subgroups of these smooth connected groups exist by [lem-sfb-smooth-connected-derived-subgroup]. Moreover $H$ is solvable: the commutator map of a subgroup factors through each corresponding ambient derived subgroup, so induction embeds $D^iH$ in $D^iB$, which is trivial for sufficiently large $i$.

source.place: Theorem 17.46, p.365, first two sentences; Corollary 13.10 and Theorem 17.38.

proof.text: Form $Q=G/B$ by [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry], with quotient map $q$. The coset formula defines left translation on $Q$ and the identity coset $o=q(1)$. The quotient is faithfully flat; its coset fibre is $G\times_QG\simeq G\times_F B$, and its sheaf quotient gives fpqc local lifts. It is of finite presentation: $q$ is of finite type by [lemma-nagata-finite-type-to-separated-target]; $Q$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian] over the field $F$ (its only ideals are $0$ and $F$); hence $q$ is locally of finite presentation by [pqf-lem-lft-fp-locnoeth], and is quasi-compact and quasi-separated by [lem-weil-pbc-qcqs-morphism-permanence], since $G$ is affine and $Q$ separated. It therefore meets the hypotheses of [lem-sfb-borel-quotient-proper-geometry], which says that $Q$ is proper and $q$ is smooth. In particular $q$ is an open surjection by [lem-weil-pbc-flat-lfp-open], using [lem-pc-smooth-flat] for flatness and local finite presentation. For the action restricted to $C$, its scheme stabilizer of $o$ is $H$: $co=o$ if and only if $c\in B$, on every algebra. The reduced orbit $O=C\cdot o$ is smooth and locally closed by [lem-sfb-smooth-group-orbit-geometry], and $O\simeq C/H$ by [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry].

source.place: Theorem 17.46, p.365: reduction to closedness of the orbit in the complete quotient.

proof.text: Prepare the solvable group $B$. Its derived series is a finite normal series with commutative quotients: the iterated derived subgroups are smooth connected closed normal subgroups by [lem-sfb-smooth-connected-derived-subgroup], and the commutator becomes trivial on each quotient. Thus the normal-series version of solvability in [lem-sfb-perfect-solvable-unipotent-torus] applies. Since $F$ is algebraically closed, it is perfect. This gives a smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup $U$ and a quotient homomorphism $\varphi:B\to D=B/U$ with $D$ a torus. Choose a maximal torus $T$ of $B$ containing $S$: tori are smooth and connected by [lem-sfb-multiplicative-type-largest-subtorus], and among tori containing $S$ a greatest-dimensional one is maximal, by the bounded integer dimensions and strict dimension growth in [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products]. By [lem-sfb-solvable-torus-complements], $\varphi|_T:T\to D$ is an isomorphism. Consequently every $b\in B(F)$ has a unique expression $b=ut$ with $u\in U(F),t\in T(F)$: set $t=(\varphi|_T)^{-1}\varphi(b)$ and $u=bt^{-1}$. Here $\ker\varphi=U$: a point in the kernel belongs to $U$ fppf locally by sheafification of cosets, and the closed equations of $U$ then vanish globally by faithful flatness.

source.place: Theorem 16.33(c),(d), p.336, and Theorem 17.46, pp.365--366: the quotient by the unipotent subgroup and choice of T.

proof.text: Let $M=q^{-1}(|O|)\subseteq |G|$. After extending a residue field to an algebraic closure, the quotient coset formulas show that $M$ is precisely the topological image of multiplication $C\times_F B\to G$: $q(g)=q(c)$ if and only if $g=cb$. The lifting clauses of [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry] justify choosing these geometric representatives; equality of geometric representatives detects the same underlying point. In particular $M$ is locally closed, since $O$ is locally closed. Let $Z$ be the reduced closed subscheme supported on the closure of $M$. The product $C\times_F B$ is connected by [lem-weil-pbc-geometrically-connected-product-components], since $C$ is geometrically connected and $B$ is connected. The continuous image and its closure are connected: a separation pulls back to a separation of the source, and a dense connected subset cannot meet two clopen pieces of its closure. Hence $Z$ is connected and contains $1$. It is affine and of finite type, being a reduced closed subscheme of the affine finite-type scheme $G$.

source.place: Theorem 17.46, p.365: connectedness of the closure of CB.

proof.text: Use [lem-sfb-constant-source-closed-factorization-locus] for the family $S\times_FG\to G$, $(s,y)\mapsto y^{-1}sy$, and the closed subgroup $B\hookrightarrow G$. Its hypotheses hold: the groups are separated over $F$ by [lem-sc-group-scheme-separated-field] and of finite type. It gives a closed subscheme $L\subseteq G$ on which this family factors through $B$. The morphism $C\times_F B\to G$ factors through $L$, since $(cb)^{-1}s(cb)=b^{-1}sb\in B$ on every algebra. Thus $M\subseteq |L|$, so also $|Z|\subseteq |L|$. As $Z$ is reduced, [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-source-factors-through-closed-subscheme] makes $Z\to G$ factor through $L$. The universal property of $L$ now gives an actual morphism $Z\times_F S\to B$, $(y,s)\mapsto y^{-1}sy$, not just a containment on rational points.

source.place: Theorem 17.46, p.365, equation (126) and footnote 2 (closed transporter).

proof.text:
Compose the family just constructed with $\varphi$ to obtain $\psi:Z\times_F S\to D$. For every algebra $A$ and $y\in Z(A)$ it is a group homomorphism in $s$, because conjugation and $\varphi$ are homomorphisms. The two tori $S$ and $D$ are diagonalizable over the algebraically closed field: $\mathbf G_m^r=D_F(\mathbf Z^r)$ by [lem-sfb-diagonalizable-group-geometric-criteria]. The parameter $Z$ is connected, affine and of finite type with the point $1$. Thus [lem-sfb-diagonalizable-hom-family-rigidity] applies, with $x_0=1$, and gives the equality of morphisms
$$\varphi(y^{-1}sy)=\varphi(s).$$
This holds for all algebra-valued points, including nonreduced algebras.

For each $b\in B(F)$, right translation $r_b:G\to G$ is a homeomorphism and preserves $M$, because $q(gb)=q(g)$ on every algebra. It therefore preserves its closure $|Z|$ and, being an isomorphism, preserves the reduced closed subscheme $Z$. In particular $y\in Z(F)$ implies $yb\in Z(F)$. This is the continuity assertion $\overline{CB}\,B\subseteq\overline{CB}$ used by Milne.

source.place: Theorem 17.46, p.366: right B-stability of the closure.

proof.text: Fix $y\in Z(F)$. By the transporter step, $S_y=y^{-1}Sy$ is a torus subgroup of $B$. Enlarge it to a maximal torus $T_y$ of $B$, using again the smoothness of tori and the greatest-dimension argument of [lem-sfb-multiplicative-type-largest-subtorus, lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products]. Apply [lem-sfb-borel-maximal-torus-conjugacy] to the smooth connected group $B$: there is $b\in B(F)$ with $b^{-1}T_yb=T$. Write $b=ut$ by step 3. Then $t^{-1}u^{-1}S_yut\subseteq T$, and conjugating by $t\in T$ gives $u^{-1}S_yu\subseteq T$. These are inclusions of subgroup schemes, because the cited maximal-torus conjugacy has that meaning. We have derived the required unipotent conjugation from existing nodes; we do not use a stronger claim hidden in a source's proof.

source.place: Theorem 17.46, p.366: the use of Theorem 16.33(d), expanded using maximal-torus conjugacy and the torus complement.

proof.text: The point $yu$ lies in $Z(F)$ by right $B$-stability. Apply the rigidity equality at $yu$. Both $(yu)^{-1}s(yu)$ and $s$ lie in $T$ after every algebra extension: the former by step 8, the latter because $S\subseteq T$. Their images under $\varphi$ agree. Since $\varphi|_T$ is an isomorphism, they are equal. Thus $yu\in C(F)$, by the all-algebra centralizer definition, and $y=(yu)u^{-1}\in C(F)B(F)\subseteq M$. We conclude $Z(F)\subseteq M$.

source.place: Theorem 17.46, p.366: injectivity on T and the conclusion y lies in CB.

proof.text: Since $M$ is locally closed and dense in its closure $|Z|$, it is open in $|Z|$; hence $|Z|\setminus M$ is closed there. If that complement were nonempty, [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space] would give a closed point of $Z$ in it, and [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base] would make it an $F$-point, contradicting step 9. Thus $M=|Z|$ is closed in $G$. The open surjection $q$ is a quotient map: if $q^{-1}(V)$ is open, then $V=q(q^{-1}(V))$ is open. Applying this to the complement of $|O|$ shows that $|O|$ is closed in $Q$. As its inclusion is already a locally closed immersion, it is a closed immersion (in an open neighbourhood use its defining ideal; outside its now closed support use the unit ideal, and these agree on the overlap). By [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-proper], $O$ is proper, since $Q$ is proper.

source.place: Theorem 17.46, pp.365--366: closedness of CB and of the orbit, hence completeness.

proof.text: It remains to prove maximality of $H$; we give the fixed-point argument behind the criterion in Milne 17.19. Suppose $H\subseteq J\subseteq C$, with $J$ smooth, connected and solvable. The proper scheme $O\simeq C/H$ is nonempty and of finite type. By [lem-sfb-solvable-proper-fixed-point], the left $J$-action on $O$ has an $F$-point fixed scheme-theoretically. Lift it to $c\in C(F)$ by [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry]. For every algebra $A$, fixedness says $jcH=cH$, so $c^{-1}Jc\subseteq H$ as subgroup schemes. The strict dimension-growth assertion of [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products] shows that $\dim J\leq\dim H$, since conjugation preserves dimension. If $H\subsetneq J$, the same assertion would give $\dim H<\dim J$, a contradiction. Hence $J=H$. Together with step 1, $H=B\cap C$ is a maximal smooth connected solvable subgroup of $C$, exactly a Borel subgroup.

source.place: Proposition 17.19, p.357, via its Borel fixed-point argument; Theorem 17.46, p.365.
